tasks.title: Earth and Moon
tasks.statement: The photo of the Earth and the Moon is taken from an artificial satellite of the Earth. Estimate the stellar magnitude of the Moon for an observer on this satellite.

parts.question: Estimate the stellar magnitude of the Moon for an observer on this satellite.
parts.reference: Let us find the distance from the satellite to the Moon using the ratio of angular radii and distances. From the equations $R_E = L_E p_E$, $R_M = L_M p_M$, and $L_M = L_{EM} + L_E$, we find the distance to the Moon from the satellite $L_M = L_{EM} / (1 - (R_E/R_M)(p_M/p_E))$. The magnitude is $m_s = m_0 + 5 \lg(L_M/L_{EM}) = m_0 - 5 \lg(1 - (R_E/R_M)(p_M/p_E))$. Measuring values from the picture or using standard values ($p_E/p_M = 80/13 = 6.15$, $L_{EM} = 384400$ km, $R_E/R_M = 3.67$, $m_0 = -12.7^m$), we get $m_s = -10.8^m$. Measuring of $p_E$, $p_M$ and correct calculations resulting in answers from $-10.6^m$ to $-11.0^m$ are accepted as correct.

tasks.title: Sidereal period
tasks.statement: Estimate (at least roughly) the smallest and the largest possible orbital sidereal periods of bodies (any bodies, including artificial ones) of our Solar System.

parts.question: Estimate the smallest and the largest possible orbital sidereal periods of bodies of our Solar System.
parts.reference: Smallest period: $T = (3\pi / G\rho)^{1/2}$. The densest bodies in our Solar System are planets of the Earth group, and an orbit around Mercury can lie just near its surface with density $\rho = 5430$ kg/m$^3$, giving $T \approx 5100$ sec $\approx 85$ min (1 pt difference recommended for solutions using only bodies rotating around the Sun, which gives $\approx 10000$ sec). Largest period: period of rotation around the Sun of a body with the maximum possible semiaxis less than a half distance to the nearest stars, i.e., about $0.6$ pc $\approx 120000$ a.e., giving $T \approx 40$ mln years (correct answers in interval from 30 to 90 mln years).

tasks.title: Mars set
tasks.statement: Estimate (at least roughly) the duration of Mars disk set for an observer at the mountain Koshka in Simeiz for Mars in Great opposition.

parts.question: Estimate the duration of Mars disk set.
parts.reference: Distance to Mars in Great opposition is $S = a_M(1 - e_M) = 57.1$ mln km. Angular size of the disk is $\alpha = D_M / S = 1.19 \times 10^{-5}$ rad $= 0.41$ arcmin. The sky moves with angular speed $\omega = 360^\circ / 86164$ sec $= 0.25$ arcmin/sec. Taking the latitude of Simeiz $\phi = 45^\circ$, the duration of Mars disk set is $\tau = \alpha / (\omega \sin \phi) = 2.3$ sec. Refraction and height do not affect the duration.

tasks.title: Photo
tasks.statement: In the photo given to you there is an airplane with the Moon in the background. Let us suppose that the photo was taken in Simeiz at the day of a solar eclipse (or at one of the days closest to a solar eclipse). Estimate how long later is (or how long time ago was) the solar eclipse. (Note: The answer «Будет-Will be» or «Было-Was» has to be written in English or Russian.) Will it be (or was it) possible to observe this eclipse in Simeiz? (Note: the answer «Да-Yes», «Может быть-May be» or «Нет-No» has to be written in English or Russian and a picture explaining your answer has to be included.)

parts.question: Estimate how long later is/ago was the solar eclipse and whether it was possible to observe it in Simeiz.
parts.reference: 1) The photo was taken around sunset (illuminated area on the right side of the moon for northern hemisphere means rising phase, so new moon was a short time ago). Answer: «Было» or «Was». 2) Measuring the illuminated area $b/R \approx 2/52$, phase $\phi = \arccos(1 - b/R) \approx 15.9^\circ$. Relative angular speed of the moon relative to the sun is $12.2^\circ$ per day, so the period since new moon is $15.9^\circ / 12.2^\circ \approx 1.30$ days $\approx 31^\circ$ hours (intervals 28-34 hours allowed). 3) Since it was shot near sunset, the solar eclipse took place in daytime on the previous day. Answer: «Может быть» or «May be» (if eclipse zone covered Simeiz).

tasks.title: Visit
tasks.statement: Extraterrestrial animals (animaloids) decided to colonize the Earth. The navigation devices of the spacecrafts of vituloids (lat. vitulus = seal = тюлень) needs that sometimes after the landing the Polar star ($a = 2^h 32^m, \delta = 89^\circ 16'$ at the epoch of starting the colonization) must be exactly in Zenith and the devices of crocodiloids needs that sometimes the Polar Star must be exactly on the Horizon. The devices are placed on the top of the spacecrafts and these can land on the Earth only in vertical positions. Also every device has to be invisible directly for the device of any other spacecraft. Estimate, how many spacecrafts of every type of animaloids can land on the Earth. Consider the Earth to be spherical, the spacecrafts’ bottoms to be on its surface (may stay either on ground or on the water) and the height of every spacecraft is h = 10 m.

parts.question: Estimate how many spacecrafts of vituloids and crocodiloids can land on the Earth.
parts.reference: Minimum distance between two spacecrafts $D = 2L = 2(R_E h)^{1/2} = 22.6$ km (where $L = (2 R_E h)^{1/2}$ for $h=10$ m). For vituloids: latitude $\phi = 89^\circ 16'$. Length of the circle $S = 2 \pi R_E \sin(90^\circ - \phi) = 512$ km. Number of vituloids: $[S/D] = [2 \pi R_E \sin(90^\circ - \phi) / (8 R_E h)^{1/2}] = 22$. For crocodiloids: whole belt near equator with length $A = 2 \pi R_E = 40076$ km and width $B = 2 \sin(90^\circ - \phi) R_E = 163.3$ km. Placed in triangular net, calculations give either $((B / (D \sqrt{3}/2)) + 1) \times (A/D) = 9 \times 1774 = 15966$ or $((B/D) + 1) \times (A / (D \sqrt{3}/2)) = 8 \times 2048 = 16384$. The second number is larger, so the answer is 16384 spacecrafts of crocodiloids.
